newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UBS looks to expand in asset management in U.S..
newsitem.headline: UBS looks to expand in asset management in U.S..

text.p: Union Bank of Switzerland is stepping up efforts to expand its asset management and private banking businesses, especially in the United States, and acquisitions are a likely part of this strategy, UBS executives said Friday.
"We must, we want to and we will play a leading role globally in this business," Chief Executive Mathis Cabiallavetta said at a news conference after UBS reported its financial results for 1996.

UBS, Switzerland's biggest bank, said it suffered a group net loss of 348 million Swiss francs ($235.7 million) last year after special provisions for credit risks and restructuring, but it said operating results were good. The loss compared with a 1995 profit of 1.68 billion ($1.14 billion).
The bank said its three principal businesses turned in good results, but the performance of its U.S. unit was still too weak.
"Our asset management company in New York has not yet found its definitive position in the U.S. market," Cabiallavetta said.
"We want to focus our efforts particularly on the expansion of our asset management business both at home and abroad ... Obviously, an acquisition is a step that cannot be ruled out entirely."

The UBS executives said the bank did not intend to expand activities across the board with a view toward becoming a global and traditional investment bank, but would adopt a more selective approach to expansion.

The fact that UBS said it did not want to become a global investment bank poured more cold water on rumours that UBS was interested in some kind of link-up with Merrill Lynch, the giant New York-based brokerage company.
UBS said that in the investment banking area it wanted to capitalise on its strength in Europe and Asia.

In the United States, it said, it wants to become a leading player in six industry segments -- health sciences, information technology, energy/natural resources, financial institutions, media/entertainment and telecommunications.
Cabiallavetta said that the bank now had its provision problems under control and expected a positive year.

Excluding the special provision and a restructuring charge of 120 million Swiss francs ($81.3 million), "group profit would have been in the region of 1.8 billion francs ($1.22 billion), 7 percent more than in 1995," UBS said.

Cabiallavetta said the bank's ordinary provisions could now be kept down to between 400 million and 600 million francs ($270 and $407 million) a year, freeing up income for profits that had been going to cover risky domestic loans.

"UBS reported a good operating result for 1996. Cash flow was increased by 21 percent to 4,312 million Swiss francs ($2.85 billion)," the bank said in a statement before Cabiallavetta's news conference.
